title: The invisible carriage and the を particle
summary: The main carriage can be hidden (the zero pronoun), and を adds a white carriage: what the action is done to.

blocks.text: In English you must always say who or what: "I", "it", "she". Japanese does not. Whenever the main carriage is clear from the situation, it is simply left out. The course calls this the **invisible carriage** (textbooks: the **zero pronoun**, or a dropped subject). It is still **there** in the grammar, you just do not say it.
（私が）先生だ。 The carriage is empty, but the train still runs.
By default the zero is **the speaker**. But context can change it: if you point at a rustling bush and say 「猫だ！」, the zero is the thing you are looking at.

blocks.en: (I) am a teacher. The zero defaults to the speaker.
(It) is a cat! The zero is what you can see.
(Today) is Monday. The zero is today.

blocks.text: The two black cars are the core. **White carriages** add information to it. The first is **を**, which marks **what the action is done to** (textbooks: the **object**; a handy memory is that を is read "o", as in object).
私がケーキを食べる。 The core is "I eat"; ケーキを says what is eaten.

blocks.en: (I) eat cake. With the main carriage dropped, the zero is "I" again.

items: A sentence cannot exist without a **が**: an action needs someone doing it, so a missing carriage is a **zero**, not a gap.
The zero is **you (the speaker)** unless the situation points to something else.
**を** marks what the action is done to. It attaches to the word **before** it.
Dropping the zero is normal and natural. Saying 私 every time sounds heavy.

questions.instruction: What does the invisible main carriage mean by default?
questions.note: With nothing else to go on, the zero is "I".

questions.instruction: Who or what is the zero?
questions.prompt: Pointing at a bush that rustles, someone says 「猫だ！」
questions.note: Context decides: here the zero is the thing the speaker is looking at.

questions.instruction: Tap the white carriage marked by を
questions.note: ケーキを is the thing being eaten.

questions.instruction: In （私が）ケーキを食べる, which part is hidden?
questions.note: The main carriage is dropped; the zero is understood.
を marks what the action is done to. The main carriage takes が.

questions.instruction: Which sentence has a hidden main carriage?
questions.note: There is no が part, so the carriage is a zero.

questions.instruction: In （今日が）月曜日だ, who or what is the zero?
questions.note: Saying 月曜日だ about the day says: (today) is Monday.

questions.instruction: Why does Japanese drop "I" so often?
options: The zero is understood from context
questions.note: The carriage is still there in the grammar; it just does not have to be spoken.

questions.instruction: Which particle marks what the action is done to?

questions.note: Same train: carriage + white carriage + engine.

questions.instruction: Which means "(I) read the book", with the subject dropped?
questions.note: 本を marks the thing read; the zero is "I".
